metadata.note: The Mount Washington Cog Railway, opened 1869, is the world's first mountain-climbing rack railway and is still operating today -- the single most famous railroad in New Hampshire. It climbs about 3 miles from Marshfield Base Station (2,700 ft elevation) to the 6,288-ft summit of Mount Washington, the highest peak in the northeastern US, on a grade as steep as 37 degrees. Geometry is real-traced from OpenStreetMap, which tags the actual rack-railway track in detail (including sidings and the engine/turntable area at Marshfield). NOTE ON TRACING: the default clustering tolerance (300m) used for most lines in this dataset produced a mathematically impossible 'shortcut' here (a computed path shorter than the straight-line distance between endpoints) because several short yard/siding ways near Marshfield Base Station chained together within that tolerance despite representing distinct track points up to ~1km apart; a much tighter 50m tolerance (appropriate for this short, dense line) resolved it to a real, connected 4.7km path, matching Wikipedia's 'approximately 3 miles' figure.

Teague (1931) -> Dartmouth College -> Arthur S. Teague (1962) -> Ellen Crawford Teague -> NH businessmen (1983) -> Wayne Presby/Joel Bedor (1986-2017))
https://www.asme.org/about-asme/engineering-history/landmarks/18-mount-washington-cog-railway (completed 1869 for $139,500; designed/built by Sylvester Marsh, a civil-mechanical engineer)
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API, overpass.openstreetmap.fr mirror): railway=narrow_gauge tagged 'Mount Washington Cog Railway' (rack=yes, gauge=1422, railway:preserved=yes), routed via Dijkstra shortest path through a graph of these real track ways (built with a 50m clustering tolerance rather than the usual 300m, to avoid over-merging the dense cluster of short yard/siding ways near Marshfield Base Station) between the Marshfield and summit endpoints.

segments.note: The world's first mountain-climbing cog (rack-and-pinion) railway, conceived and built by Sylvester Marsh. First paying passengers rode partway up August 14, 1868; construction reached the 6,288-foot summit in July 1869, with the first through train August 29, 1869. Climbs about 3 miles up Mount Washington's western slope from Marshfield Base Station (2,700 ft) at an average grade of 1 foot in 4 (max ~37 degrees) via Jacob's Ladder. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: Sold to Henry N. Teague in 1931; later owners included Dartmouth College, Arthur S. Teague (1962), Ellen Crawford Teague, a group of New Hampshire businessmen (1983), and Wayne Presby/Joel Bedor (1986-2017). Still in continuous operation today (biodiesel and steam locomotives), with service interruptions historically only during the World Wars; winter service resumed in 2020 after facility improvements. Frequency estimated, unsourced -- this is a still-operating tourist railway, not a defunct historical line.
